name: Must Improve Over Time
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Improvement Curve
lesson.summary: This section explains the second GPT test ,  that a technology must get cheaper and more capable over time ,  and shows why quantum computing's progress so far doesn't clearly satisfy it.
lesson.body:
You already know that a general-purpose technology has to be pervasive and enable new products or methods across many industries. But being useful once isn't enough ,  a true GPT has to keep getting better, year after year, in a way that opens doors it couldn't open before. That's the second criterion: a steady trajectory of rising capability and falling cost, not a one-time leap.

The reason this trajectory matters is that it creates a feedback loop. As a technology improves, more people find it worth adopting; wider adoption brings more investment, more manufacturing scale, and more accumulated know-how; and that, in turn, drives the next round of improvement. Classic computing is the textbook case: transistor density on chips roughly doubled every couple of years for decades, a pattern known as Moore's Law, and the resulting collapse in the cost of computation is what let computers move from room-sized mainframes to devices in everyone's pocket. Each cost drop didn't just make the old uses cheaper ,  it made entirely new uses economically possible. That compounding is the actual mechanism behind "general purpose": it's not the technology's usefulness at one moment, it's the direction and rate of change.

Now apply that lens to quantum computing. If it were on a genuine GPT trajectory, you'd expect several things moving together: more qubits, yes, but also lower error rates, longer coherence times (how long a qubit holds its quantum state before noise destroys it), and a falling cost per unit of trustworthy computation ,  all reinforcing each other and steadily widening the set of problems worth running on a quantum machine. What's actually happened is more lopsided. Qubit counts have risen, but error rates and coherence times have only inched forward, and there's no clear evidence that the cost of getting a useful, reliable answer out of a quantum computer has been dropping the way the cost of a classical calculation did.

This distinction matters because raw qubit count is a misleading headline number on its own. A physical qubit is noisy ,  it's disturbed by tiny amounts of heat, stray electromagnetic fields, or imperfect control pulses ,  so a single qubit's raw state isn't trustworthy for a real computation. Getting a reliable "logical" qubit typically requires combining and error-correcting many physical qubits together. If you add physical qubits without also cutting the error rate per qubit, you haven't necessarily added computational power that anyone can use ,  you may just have more unreliable parts. That's why the improvement curve for quantum computing looks so different from the one that carried classical computing from labs into everyday life: growth in one number (qubit count) hasn't been matched by growth in the number that actually governs usefulness (trustworthy computation per dollar).

None of this means quantum computing is a dead end ,  the underlying physics and engineering are still advancing. But the GPT criterion isn't asking whether a technology is impressive today; it's asking whether it's on a track of compounding, cost-lowering improvement that keeps unlocking new applications. On the evidence so far, quantum computing hasn't demonstrated that track record, which is exactly why this second criterion is the harder one for it to clear.
